video_metadata.working_title: IDAHO 1996 Cold Case Solved After 23 Years — Justice for Angie Dodge
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: An 18-year-old is raped and killed in her first apartment in Idaho Falls in 1996; police extract a false confession from a 20-year-old who spends 20 years in prison, until the victim's own mother pushes genetic genealogy to find the real killer, the man who lived across the street.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into outrage at a broken system, then hope through a mother's persistence and science

protagonist._instructions: Main character: in this story the moral protagonist is Carol Dodge; the perpetrator is Brian Leigh Dripps Sr. Both summarized.
protagonist.full_name: Carol Dodge (mother of Angie Raye Dodge); perpetrator: Brian Leigh Dripps Sr.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Carol: age not verified. Dripps: 53 at arrest (May 15, 2019), 55 at sentencing (June 8, 2021); by those figures he was 30 in June 1996 (derived, not directly reported).
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Carol: mother, advocate, co-founder with son Brent of the '5 for HOPE' fundraising for cold-case foundations and police. Dripps: lived across the street from Angie in 1996; later of Caldwell, Idaho; now serving 20-years-to-life in Idaho prison.
protagonist.location: Idaho Falls, Bonneville County, eastern Idaho; Dripps later in Caldwell, Canyon County.
protagonist.physical_description: Not used (avoid). Parabon's 2017 predicted phenotype for the perpetrator: Northern European ancestry, fair skin, brown eyes, brown hair (one account).
protagonist.background_brief: Carol believed police for years that Christopher Tapp was guilty; she later concluded he was innocent, supported his exoneration, and pushed CeCe Moore and Parabon NanoLabs to try genetic genealogy on the degraded sample in November 2018.
protagonist.psychological_profile: Do not speculate. Documented: relentless persistence, publicly described as a '20-year crusade' (ABC News).
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: Carol and son Brent ask people to honor Angie by donating to '5 for HOPE' to help cold-case foundations and under-funded police departments.
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: Dripps: 'Brian Dripps Sr.'; Angie's middle name Raye.

individuals.name: Angie Raye Dodge
individuals.role_or_profession: 18; Idaho Falls High School graduate (1995, with honors), briefly at Idaho State University; worked at Beauty for All Seasons
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Daughter of Carol Dodge; murdered by Brian Dripps, her neighbor across the street
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Raped and stabbed to death in her apartment at 444 I Street on June 13, 1996
individuals.humanizing_detail: Only daughter, youngest of four; tutored children in reading/math; loved camping and starting water fights with cousins; artistic, wrote poetry; dreamed of becoming an entrepreneur (family tribute)

individuals.name: Christopher 'Chris' Tapp
individuals.role_or_profession: 20 in January 1997; wrongfully convicted; exonerated July 17, 2019; later advocate
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Falsely confessed after coercive interrogations; Carol Dodge came to support his innocence
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: About 20 years in prison (1997-2017) for a crime he did not commit; died Nov 5, 2023 at 47 after an altercation in Las Vegas
individuals.humanizing_detail: Lobbied for Idaho's wrongful-conviction compensation law and testified in several states against deceptive interrogation tactics (Innocence Project)
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: No verified direct quote gathered in this session.

individuals.name: Carol Dodge
individuals.humanizing_detail: Changed her mind about Tapp; pushed for genealogy
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: We had to go through 25 years of hell. / Whatever you give this man is not enough. / You have shattered our family.

individuals.name: Todd Dodge
individuals.humanizing_detail: Asked judge to reject the plea so Dripps would face a jury
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: he sentenced me to a lifetime of hell. And so far, I have served 9,126 days.

individuals.name: Brent Dodge
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Was at the police department when family was called to identify Angie (one account)
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: I wouldn't say it's closure because as Todd described there is still a lot of chaos.

individuals.name: Michael Usry Jr.
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Wrongly suspected via 2014 familial Y-DNA search
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Questioned, gave DNA, cleared about a month later

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Dodge family; Tapp and his family; Usry family; Hobbs and Sargis (suspected, never charged in this crime)

characters.name: Jared Fuhriman
characters.role_in_story: Idaho Falls police officer/detective who interrogated Tapp; former school resource officer Tapp trusted; later mayor of Idaho Falls; died at 60 after a long battle with Alzheimer's (date not verified)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Testified at 1998 trial that officers did not feed Tapp information; recordings later showed otherwise (per later reviews); testified at Feb 29, 2012 hearing as mayor

characters.name: Ben Hobbs
characters.role_in_story: Original suspect; arrested in Nevada on a separate charge; never charged in Angie's death; DNA excluded

characters.name: Jeremy Sargis
characters.role_in_story: Second man added to police theory; DNA not a match; never charged

characters.name: CeCe Moore
characters.key_actions_they_took: Built family trees from a degraded sample at Carol Dodge's urging; found the Dripps branch
characters.notable_quotes: Said genealogy had never been done in a suspect case with such a degraded sample (paraphrase, not exact quote).

characters.name: Detective Sage Albright
characters.role_in_story: Idaho Falls detective; wrote probable cause affidavit

characters.name: Daniel (Danny) Clark
characters.key_actions_they_took: 2016 review found no reason to reverse; July 17, 2019 filed to exonerate Tapp

characters.name: John Thomas
characters.role_in_story: Tapp's attorney who negotiated the 2017 release

characters.name: Judge Joel Tingey
characters.role_in_story: Seventh District judge; took Dripps' plea and sentenced him

characters.name: Deputy Attorney General Jessica Kuehn
characters.key_actions_they_took: Argued Dripps lived 23 years knowing he killed Dodge and never came forward (paraphrase)

characters.name: Daniel Rodimer
characters.role_in_story: Former pro wrestler and former Nevada congressional candidate charged with murder in Tapp's 2023 death; pleaded not guilty; has NOT been convicted; trial reported set for Feb 1, 2027

events.what_happened: Angie Raye Dodge is born; the only daughter and youngest of four children.
events.significance: Victim's birth; she will be 18 at her death.

events.location: San Diego, California; then Idaho Falls, Idaho
events.what_happened: Angie begins preschool in San Diego and continues through grade school, junior high and high school in Idaho Falls; tutors younger children in math and English/reading.
Angie graduates with honors, then attends Idaho State University (ISU) for a short time.
events.significance: Portrait. NOTE: one weak source [54] says she 'had just graduated' in May 1996; family tribute says 1995 - use 1995.

events.what_happened: Angie, 18, lives in her first apartment and works at Beauty for All Seasons.
events.significance: Setting; the apartment where she is killed.

events.what_happened: Angie is raped and stabbed to death in her apartment. She does not show up for work.
Coworkers worried that she had not come to work go to the apartment; one account says a friend/coworker entered the unlocked apartment and called 911; Angie is found dead.
events.significance: Discovery. Exact finder names not verified.

events.what_happened: The family is called to the police department to identify Angie; her brother Brent is there (one account).
Ben Hobbs becomes the original suspect; he is arrested in Nevada on a separate charge and serves time there for a separate attack. He is never charged in Angie's death; DNA eliminates him.
Christopher Tapp, 20, a friend of Hobbs, is first interviewed by Idaho Falls police and released.

Tapp is questioned repeatedly, including through polygraph examinations; officers including Jared Fuhriman feed him details of the case and tell him he could face the death penalty unless he implicates himself and another suspect. One source says the questioning totalled about 20 hours (single-sourced).
An interrogation of Tapp later becomes the sole focus of a 2012 evidentiary hearing.

Tapp's fifth polygraph. He is told he might get a more lenient sentence if he had been in fear for his life; the examiner says he was 'deceptive' but 'passed'. Tapp then says he cut Dodge because Hobbs had threatened to kill him.
With DNA excluding Hobbs, police theory expands to include Jeremy Sargis and then a third, never-identified man; Sargis's DNA also does not match.

events.location: Seventh Judicial District Court, Bonneville County
events.what_happened: Tapp's trial begins. Fuhriman testifies officers did not reveal information to Tapp; later reviews of the videos showed otherwise.
After about 13 hours of deliberation, the jury finds Tapp guilty of rape and first-degree murder although his DNA did not match the crime-scene sample.

The judge declines the death penalty and sentences Tapp to 30 years to life (Marshall Project; NBC gives 40 years - conflict). Judge: 'had Mr. Tapp not confessed, there would have been no conviction in this case.'
The Idaho Innocence Project agrees to take Tapp's case.
events.significance: Start of the fight to free him.

events.what_happened: The Idaho Innocence Project requests DNA testing on hairs recovered from the scene.
A state law gives defendants greater post-conviction access to DNA evidence; the Idaho Innocence Project supported it.
Evidentiary hearing on the confession: Tapp's former attorney and Jared Fuhriman, by then mayor of Idaho Falls, take the stand.
A judge turns down the request for additional testing; later that year limited testing excludes Tapp and Hobbs as contributors.

events.location: Idaho Falls / Sorenson database via Ancestry
events.what_happened: Police find a 34-of-35 Y-chromosome marker match to Michael Usry Sr. in a Sorenson database (obtained from Ancestry with a court order); his son, New Orleans filmmaker Michael Usry Jr., is questioned, gives DNA, and is cleared about a month later (reported 2015).
A Judges for Justice review concludes Tapp's confession was coerced and did not match the physical evidence.
Prosecutor Daniel (Danny) Clark hires a private firm to review the case; in December he says he found no evidence reversing the conviction.
Tapp is released. Under a deal negotiated by attorney John Thomas, his rape conviction is vacated and he is released on time served for murder, giving up further appeals.
Idaho Falls police use Parabon's Snapshot DNA phenotyping: a composite predicting ancestry, eye, hair, skin color, freckling and face shape at default age 25 and BMI 22.
events.significance: First step of the new science.

events.what_happened: Police announce Parabon kinship analysis is 87.63 percent confident the crime-scene DNA does not match the Usry family.
Carol Dodge reaches out to genetic genealogist CeCe Moore and urges her to take the case.

Despite a degraded sample (about 61 percent of the data usually needed), Moore's team uploads the profile to GEDmatch, builds three family trees that converge on one couple (apparent great-grandparents of the perpetrator), narrows to about six men, all excluded by discarded-item DNA; the break is a son conceived shortly before a divorce who took his stepfather's surname: Brian Dripps.

Police surveil Dripps; in the first hour he flips a cigarette butt from his vehicle but it is lost in traffic; after more than 20 hours of surveillance he discards another; the Idaho State Police lab matches it to the crime-scene DNA.

Brian Leigh Dripps, 53, is arrested and charged with first-degree murder and rape. In an interview he first denies involvement, then, confronted with the DNA result, admits entering the apartment alone with a knife intending to rape her, says he did not mean to kill her, and believes she was alive when he left (affidavit by Detective Sage Albright).
Dripps is arraigned by video and denied bail; his attorney argues he is a 'kind, loving father'. Reports note he lived across the street from Angie in 1996 and was never asked for DNA.
Prosecutors file notice to seek the death penalty against Dripps.
National report: in an apparent first, genetic genealogy aids a wrongful-conviction case.

Prosecutor Daniel Clark files to clear Tapp, writing there is 'clear and convincing evidence' he was convicted of a crime he did not commit; a judge vacates the remaining conviction. Tapp is exonerated.
events.significance: Exoneration; the Innocence Project calls him the first person in the world proven innocent with genetic genealogy.

events.what_happened: Dripps' trial is set for 2021; defense says it will seek a change of venue.
Defense asks for Dripps' release from jail because of COVID-19.
events.significance: Delay; denied/not granted (he remained in custody through plea).

events.what_happened: Tapp sues the City of Idaho Falls and several former officers.
Dripps pleads guilty to first-degree murder and rape before Judge Joel Tingey under a plea deal: fixed 20 years, up to life; the death penalty is off the table.
Judge Joel Tingey sentences Dripps, 55, to 20 years to life, credit for about two years served, sex-offender registration, $10,000 in fines. Family members deliver impact statements.
Council unanimously approves an $11.7 million settlement with Tapp, paid by the city's insurer, plus a formal apology letter and a public discussion on interrogation techniques; the mayor apologizes.
Tapp is injured during an altercation at a party in a resort suite; first reported as an accident.
Christopher Tapp dies at 47. Clark County coroner later rules the death a homicide from blunt force trauma to the head.
Tribute calls Tapp 'the first person in the world to be proven innocent with genetic genealogy' and notes his advocacy for an Idaho compensation law and against deceptive interrogation.
Tapp's legal team (later his mother and estate) files a wrongful-death suit against the resort and others.
Police obtain a murder warrant for Daniel Rodimer, 45, former pro wrestler and former Nevada congressional candidate; he surrenders and later pleads not guilty.
Rodimer's attorneys move to dismiss, arguing the coroner's findings show injuries resulted from drug and alcohol use.
Judge denies Rodimer's motion to dismiss the indictment; trial reported set for February 1, 2027 (originally June 15, 2026).

the_moment.what_is_happening: Coworkers worried that 18-year-old Angie Dodge has not come to work go to her apartment and find her dead.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: The killer left his DNA; it would not match the man convicted. The real killer lived across the street.
the_moment.ironic_twist: The victim's own mother became the strongest voice for the innocent man convicted of killing her daughter.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: If the DNA never matched the man in prison, whose was it, and why did it take 23 years to find him?

the_method.technique_name: Investigative genetic genealogy (IGG) plus DNA phenotyping (Parabon NanoLabs)
step_by_step_explanation: Crime-scene DNA (semen) had a standard forensic profile that never matched anyone in CODIS.
2014: a familial Y-chromosome search of a Sorenson genealogy database produced a near match (34 of 35 markers) to the Usry family - a false lead.
2017: Parabon Snapshot phenotyping predicted ancestry and traits and produced a composite; kinship analysis cleared the Usry family (87.63 percent confidence).
Nov 2018: Carol Dodge contacts CeCe Moore. The sample is degraded: about 61 percent of the SNP data usually needed.
The SNP profile is uploaded to GEDmatch; partial matches (distant cousins) are used to build three family trees, which converge on one couple who appear to be the perpetrator's great-grandparents.
Researchers narrow to about six men in the descendants; police collect discarded items; none match.
Moore realizes one woman conceived a son shortly before divorcing; the boy took his stepfather's surname - Dripps - so he was invisible in the trees.
Surveillance: a first cigarette butt is lost in traffic; after more than 20 hours a second is collected; the state lab matches it to the crime-scene DNA.
Confirmation after arrest by a full match to the CODIS profile.
the_method.why_it_worked: Genealogy databases let investigators find relatives of an unknown person when the person himself is in no police database; persistence by the victim's mother pushed the lab to try a sample it considered too degraded.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: The FBI-run DNA index of profiles from offenders and crime scenes; a match only works if the person is already in it.
Looks only at the father-to-son line; many men in a family share it, so it points to a surname, not a person - and can mislead.
Hundreds of thousands of single-letter spelling differences in DNA; consumer genealogy tests read them to measure how related two people are.
A public site where people upload their genealogy DNA to find relatives; investigators used it in the 2018 Golden State Killer case.
Predicts likely ancestry and features such as eye and hair color from DNA; age and weight cannot be read, so defaults (25, BMI 22) are used.
Police may collect an item a person throws away in public, like a cigarette butt, and test it.

the_method.scale_of_operation: About 850,000 SNPs typically read; roughly 329,000 missing in this sample (one source); about 6-7 candidate men; more than 20 hours of surveillance.

systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Idaho Falls Police Department interrogation practices; the prosecution and courts that upheld a confession contradicted by DNA.
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Find the person whose DNA was at the scene; test confessions against physical evidence.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: Tunnel vision on Hobbs and his friends; repeated interrogations and polygraphs with threats of the death penalty and fed details; when DNA excluded suspects the theory expanded to new unidentified men instead of being dropped.
specific_incompetence_examples: Tapp's DNA did not match and no physical evidence tied him to the crime, yet he was convicted (1998).
Five polygraphs by Jan 30, 1997; examiner told him he was 'deceptive' but 'passed'.
Officer testified no details were fed; recordings later showed otherwise (per reviews).
Theory expanded from Hobbs to Sargis to a never-identified third man as each DNA test excluded them.
August 2012 a judge refused additional testing; 2016 prosecutor's review found no reason to reverse.
The real killer lived across the street and was never asked for DNA in 1996.
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The officer who helped obtain the confession, Jared Fuhriman, was mayor of Idaho Falls when he took the stand at the 2012 hearing; in 2022 the city paid $11.7 million and its mayor apologized.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Idaho Falls Police Department, with Parabon NanoLabs (CeCe Moore) and the Idaho State Police forensic lab
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: That Ben Hobbs and his friends (Tapp, then Sargis, then an unknown man) were responsible.
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Genetic genealogy (2018-2019) revealed a son who carried his stepfather's surname.
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Dripps flicked a cigarette butt out of his vehicle window during police surveillance.

the_confrontation.scene_description: Dripps, 53, is arrested and interviewed; he first denies ever being in the apartment, then is confronted with the DNA test result.
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: Admitted he entered alone with a knife intending to rape her; said he did not mean to kill her; said he wore gloves and believed she was alive when he left (affidavit).
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: Defense attorney described him as a 'kind, loving father'; he had lived across the street from the victim.

legal_resolution.trial_date_if_applicable: No trial: guilty plea Feb 9, 2021 (trial had been set for 2021).
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Plea: 'When I went over, I went with the intent to just rape her.' 'I didn't mean to murder her.'

victim_impact_statements.key_quote: We had to go through 25 years of hell.
And so far, I have served 9,126 days.

legal_resolution.sentence_received: June 8, 2021: fixed 20 years to life in prison; credit for about two years served; sex-offender registration; $10,000 fines. Both sides said that, due to poor health, 20 years was effectively a life sentence.
legal_resolution.protagonist_statement_in_court: I know you'll never forgive me, but I'm sorry.
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: Dripps remains in Idaho prison; no appeal or death reported in any source found. One unverified page lists parole eligibility May 16, 2039. Tapp: exonerated July 17, 2019; died Nov 5, 2023 (homicide ruling); Daniel Rodimer charged with murder, pleaded not guilty, motion to dismiss denied July 2026, trial reported set for Feb 1, 2027 - has not been convicted.

details: The killer lived across the street from Angie and was never asked for DNA.
The victim's mother became one of the strongest supporters of the man convicted of killing her daughter.
The officer central to the confession later became the city's mayor and testified as mayor in 2012.
A polygraph examiner told Tapp he was 'deceptive' but had 'passed'.
Dripps' 20-years-to-life sentence was lower than the one Tapp received in 1998 (Post Register).
Tapp was released in 2017 still legally a convicted murderer; he was exonerated only after the real killer was found.
The first person in the world exonerated with genetic genealogy died violently four years later; the man charged has not been convicted.

Southwest Idaho, Canyon County; Dripps' home at arrest.
Resort on the Las Vegas Strip where Tapp was fatally injured during a party in a suite.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: A confession can be produced by pressure; DNA that does not fit should stop a case, not be explained away.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Tapp was a 20-year-old who trusted an officer he knew; anyone questioned for hours under threat of execution can say what investigators want to hear.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Physical evidence outranks a story; and one person who keeps asking can move an entire system.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Genetic genealogy and its privacy debate; reform of interrogation practices; Idaho wrongful-conviction compensation.

items: 1996 was a U.S. presidential election year; the Summer Olympics were held in Atlanta beginning July 19, 1996.
In 1996 most people had no cell phone; communication ran through landlines, answering machines and pagers; home internet was mostly dial-up.
The FBI's national DNA index (NDIS, part of CODIS) began operating nationally in October 1998.
GEDmatch, a free site where people upload genealogy DNA files, launched in 2010.

The Golden State Killer case: Joseph James DeAngelo was arrested in California in April 2018 after investigators used genetic genealogy via GEDmatch; widely cited as the landmark case (also referenced in coverage of the Dodge case).
Idaho Falls is in eastern Idaho on the Snake River and is the seat of Bonneville County; Idaho State University is in Pocatello; Caldwell is in Canyon County in southwest Idaho.
Angie was 18 years and about 6 months old (Dec 21, 1977 - June 13, 1996): an adult for less than six months.
